The Dangerous Allure of Endless Progress (D.E.A.P.).

A Substack by Miles Mercer.

In a world that always wants the next bigger, faster, smarter thing, it’s getting harder to ask one simple question: When is enough?
This piece looks at our restless drive to keep improving everything—and the hidden price we’re paying in our bodies, our families, and our planet. It imagines what could happen if we chose to step back toward reality: real connections, real health, and a future where we still choose to bring new life into the world.
It’s not about stopping all progress. It’s about making sure progress still serves real human life instead of quietly replacing it. I hope it gets you thinking—and maybe even talking—about the kind of world we actually want.

The Dangerous Allure of Endless Progress (D.E.A.P.)

We humans never seem to sit still. From the first stone tools to today’s smartphones, we’re always pushing for something faster, sleeker, and “better.” We don’t do it just to survive. We do it because stopping feels like giving up. A car that goes a little quicker. A new phone with one more cool feature. It all sounds exciting—until you notice we’re hooked on the chase. The finish line keeps moving, and we keep running after it.
This endless push comes with a cost. To keep making things “better,” we dig deeper for resources, build more factories, and fill the world with chemicals from our products and waste. Rivers get dirty. The air gets heavier. And something quieter but more serious is happening inside us. More and more couples are struggling to have babies. Men’s sperm isn’t as strong as it used to be. Women’s bodies are finding it harder to carry life. We’ve created a world so full of man-made stuff that nature itself is starting to push back.
The tough question almost no one wants to ask out loud is this: When is enough?
Why can’t we agree, as regular people and as nations, to say “this is good enough” for a while? Why not spend some of that same clever energy cleaning up our rivers, growing healthier food, and making sure the air is safe to breathe? The truth is uncomfortable. For us, stopping feels like losing. Standing still feels like dying. So we keep speeding up, even as the damage piles up behind us.
Now artificial intelligence is stepping in with machines that feel almost human—soft to the touch, helpful in every way, never tired, never complaining. They can keep us company, do our chores, even act like perfect partners. Why go through the mess and worry of dating, pregnancy, and raising kids when a machine can give you comfort without any of the real-life hassle? Birth rates are already dropping fast in many countries, not because of war or poverty, but because people are quietly choosing easier paths.
We’re heading toward a fork in the road.
One path leads to a comfortable kind of ending. We enjoy pleasure without the hard work of creating the next generation. Everything runs smoothly, the screens stay bright, but the cradles go empty. Eventually the lights stay on for no one.
The other path is stranger. We don’t vanish—we blend with the machines. Our bodies change. We become thinner, with bigger heads and sharper minds hooked straight into the digital world. We start to look like the aliens we once imagined: smart, delicate, less tied to messy human biology. We don’t get taken over by outsiders. We simply improve ourselves until the old version of humanity feels outdated.
But maybe there’s a third way starting to grow—a return to enough, a coming back to reality. Think of it like the hippie movement years ago, when people pushed back against rigid rules and chased freer, more natural ways of living and loving. Today, a similar spirit could rise, but with a different focus: choosing real human connection over perfect digital versions, slower days instead of constant upgrades, and protecting our ability to have children and live healthy lives instead of outsourcing everything to machines and chemicals. It would be a gentle rebellion—not against progress itself, but against the idea that we must always have more, faster, better. A movement that says real bodies, real relationships, and real nature are worth fighting for.
We still have the same deep human spark that built beautiful things in the past. We can choose to say “enough” without losing our curiosity. We can keep exploring and inventing, but make sure the next step actually helps life instead of quietly replacing it. We can clean the rivers again. We can make having kids feel natural and hopeful once more. We can keep technology as a helpful tool instead of letting it become the main character in our story.
The real question isn’t whether we will change. We always do. The real question is whether we will change on purpose—moving toward a world that feels alive and connected—or whether we will keep racing forward until we run right off the edge, leaving behind a quiet, empty future lit only by our own machines.
The hour is late, but the river is still flowing. The choice is still ours—if we’re brave enough to take it and return to what’s real.

I've lived in South Korea for 8 years as a foreigner now. I think I start to grasp what the root of the problem is. The problem is too complex to address in one comment, but I'll try.
The convergence of liberalism and capitalism with the traditional values of Confucianism is a deadly combination rooted in materialism and abundance mentality. It always is deadly to overlap ideologies because every society has been forming over eons to be what it is, so it has its own distinct methods of survival and proliferation that are often contradicting. Korea is traditionally collectivistic society that originally had a lot of old-fashioned family values and unwritten rules, for example a standard age for marrying and even arranged marriages. As people very dependent on rice, which can only be grown in groups and communes, Koreans have always tried to be about family and society. However, capitalism and liberalism bring individualism, which isn't a bad thing, but it should be taken in step by step because it's not easy to have and nurture empathy and human connection in an individualistic society. The USA does it by the culture of small talks, family gatherings, and encouraging families or groups to be formed. Many Americans for example live with roommates because a single apartment is simply too expensive. I sometimes think that with the comfort of liberalism and capitalism you should also take the discomfort to balance it out.

South Korea built the family culture and people's empathy by things like "눈치", in other words an unspoken code of conduct that dictates how you behave in public. It's like a very subtle empathy code, where you should know things like not making too much noise or offering help to strangers in certain situations. Capitalism, liberalism, and technology killed or reduced it, leaving only negative parts of 눈치 behind. Nowadays nobody offers seats to elderly because "in Europe they don't do it". Nobody talks to strangers because there's no small talk culture. It's evident from tiny things like they don't even say pless you when you sneeze. You almost never know who your neighbors are when you're young and live separately because most probably you live in a one-room. The one room rent is at around $300-600 a month depending on location, so you never need a roomie. A lot of people don't go out of their rooms becoming like Japanese hikikomori. At the same time, the notion of "I can marry when I want to, now I want to live for myself" takes over, resulting in the average age of marriage being above 30 here, which is of course detrimental for the fertility. The parents can't get a hold of their children because "in the West they never hit their children", but as we know physical punishments were a big part of Asian upbringing, so the parents don't know how to replace it. In the West, you can ground your kid for wrongdoing, but in Korea it's not a punishment at all since the kid can just play PC games or read Naver Webtoon alone because the friendships between young people no longer revolve around physical proximity, but rather around having the same interests and tastes in fashion or content or games, etc.

All in all, it's a huge Pandora box at all levels because there are new and new problems introduced to the society at every level. There's a fundamental flaw with the "I will talk to everybody" stance that Lex takes, and I feel like as an engineer he should understand this.

If we take what he's saying at face value and assume no hidden motives, the philosophy behind this seems to be that everyone deserves to be heard and that the "marketplace of ideas" will sort out who is right and who is wrong, who has good ideas and who has bad ones.

But *who we choose to listen to* is precisely the sorting mechanism that this marketplace relies on. It really does matter who we give a "platform" to! If you control the microphone, Lex, and you give equal time to opinion A and opinion B, then you are in effect casting your vote that opinion s A and B are of equal value in this marketplace of ideas. And as a person with a very big microphone, your vote counts way more than mine. At most, I can stop watching your podcast - which, more and more, I am choosing to do - and that loss of a single viewer is such a small drop in the bucket as to be negligible.

But really it's worse than this. Because we don't just get "equal" representation of ideas. It is precisely those people who are *losing* in the marketplace of ideas who are more likely to want to inject themselves into in these conversations. Would Tucker have done this interview when he was still the top guy at Fox? Probably not. And so what happens is that the control function you put in place for selecting guests, in combination with the pressures on the supply side (who *wants* to be a guest) pushes the overall system further and further toward people with low-value ideas who strongly want those ideas to be propagated.
